prompt: Your fan-out fleet's Kafka consumer lag reaches **10 minutes** during a global sporting final. Which mitigations are reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skip fan-out to followers who haven't been active for 30 days, rebuilding their timelines by pull when they return.
options.explanation: Correct when returning-user rebuilds are reliable. Measure the inactive fraction and saved work rather than assuming a universal platform distribution.

options.text: Temporarily lower the celebrity threshold so more high-follower accounts are pulled at read time instead of pushed.
options.explanation: Correct with an overlap/deduplication transition and enough read capacity. This trades background inserts for additional foreground reads.

options.text: Prioritise fan-out to followers who are currently online.
options.explanation: Correct. It can reduce delay for readers likely to look soon, without guaranteeing that lag is invisible.

options.text: Make the post API wait until fan-out completes before returning success.
options.explanation: Incorrect. That makes authors wait minutes for a 'posted' confirmation and creates timeouts and retries (which generate *more* work). Fan-out must stay asynchronous.

options.text: Drop posts that are older than 1 minute from the fan-out queue.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Followers would silently never see those posts in their precomputed timelines. Lag is temporary; data loss is permanent.

workedExample: Measure which accounts and followers generate work, prioritise active readers, and shift selected large accounts to pull with safe transition handling. Returning users need a rebuild path. Scale consumers only within downstream capacity, and preserve durable posts and recoverable work rather than silently discarding them.

link.title: High Scalability: the architecture Twitter uses to deal with 150M active users

prompt: Most reads only inspect recent feed entries, and many accounts are inactive. What is the trade-off in keeping shorter cached timelines only for recently active users?

options.text: Less cache memory, but deeper pages and returning users need a recoverable slower path whose load must be measured.
options.explanation: Correct. Memory savings shift work to misses and rebuilds rather than eliminating it.

options.text: No trade-off: old posts can be discarded from canonical storage.
options.explanation: A cache cap does not change the history-retention contract.

options.text: Every read becomes faster, including a returning user’s cold rebuild.
options.explanation: Cold reconstruction can be slower and can stress the graph and post stores.

options.text: Replicas are no longer useful because timelines are derived.
options.explanation: Derivability permits recovery but does not make simultaneous cache loss cheap.

workedExample: Cache the frequently read portion, retain authoritative posts and graph data, and define how a missing or deep page is rebuilt. Coordinate that rebuild with concurrent fan-out so new inserts are not overwritten. Measure returning-user latency and rebuild storms as well as memory savings.
